name: Web Fundamentals
description: How a page loads, the browser rendering pipeline, storage, the same-origin policy, CORS and Core Web Vitals.

modules.name: The Big Picture
modules.description: What Web Fundamentals is, what it is for, and the words everything else builds on.

cards.prompt: The internet vs the World Wide Web
cards.answer: The internet is the global network of connected computers; the web is one service that runs on top of it — pages and resources linked together and fetched over HTTP.

right.title: World Wide Web
points: Pages and resources linked by URLs
Accessed with web browsers over HTTP

cards.explanation: People use the words interchangeably, but email or an online game uses the internet without using the web.

cards.prompt: What are a client and a server on the web?
cards.answer: The client (usually a browser) sends requests; the server is a program on another machine that receives them and sends back responses — an HTML page, an image, some JSON.
cards.explanation: Front-end code runs on the client and back-end code runs on the server. One machine can be both; the words describe roles in a conversation, not types of hardware.

cards.prompt: What are the parts of a URL?
cards.answer: In `https://shop.example.com:443/products/42?sort=price#reviews`: scheme (`https`), host or domain (`shop.example.com`), port (`443`, usually implied), path (`/products/42`), query string (`?sort=price`) and fragment (`#reviews`, handled only by the browser).
cards.explanation: A URL (Uniform Resource Locator) tells the browser which protocol to use, which server to contact and which resource to ask for.

cards.prompt: What is HTTP?
cards.answer: HyperText Transfer Protocol: the request–response protocol browsers and servers use to exchange web content. A request has a method (`GET`, `POST` …), a URL and headers; the response has a status code (`200 OK`, `404 Not Found`), headers and a body.
cards.explanation: HTTPS is HTTP sent over an encrypted TLS connection; today almost all web traffic is HTTPS. HTTP itself is stateless — each request stands alone, which is why cookies exist.

cards.prompt: What does DNS do?
cards.answer: The Domain Name System translates human-friendly names such as `example.com` into the IP addresses computers use to connect — the internet's phone book.
cards.explanation: Every visit to a new domain starts with a DNS lookup, and answers are cached at many levels to keep it fast. When "the site is down" for some people but not others, DNS is a common culprit.

cards.prompt: At a high level, what happens when you open a web page?
cards.answer: The browser looks up the domain via DNS, opens a secure connection to the server, sends an HTTP request, receives HTML, then fetches the CSS, JavaScript and images it references, and finally renders and runs them to draw the page.
cards.explanation: Every step costs time, which is why web performance work focuses on fewer and smaller requests, caching and getting the first useful content on screen quickly.

modules.name: Loading & Rendering
modules.description: What happens between typing a URL and seeing pixels.

cards.prompt: Walk through what happens when you type a URL and press Enter.
cards.answer: DNS resolution → TCP (or QUIC) connection → TLS handshake → HTTP request → response → HTML parsed into the DOM, CSS into the CSSOM → render tree → layout → paint → composite. Subresources are fetched as the parser discovers them, and JavaScript may block parsing.
cards.explanation: This question is really about depth: any single step (DNS caching, TLS session resumption, HTTP/2 multiplexing, the preload scanner, critical rendering path) can be expanded. Knowing the shape tells you where a slow page is actually losing time.

resources.title: MDN — Populating the page: how browsers work

cards.prompt: `<script>` vs `defer` vs `async`
cards.answer: Plain scripts block parsing; `defer` downloads in parallel and runs after parsing in document order; `async` downloads in parallel and runs as soon as it lands, in any order.

left.title: defer
points: The right default for app code

cards.explanation: A blocking script in `<head>` stalls the parser, delaying first paint. `type="module"` is deferred by default. Anything that must run before paint (theme flash prevention) is the rare legitimate blocking script — keep it inline and tiny.

cards.prompt: What are the Core Web Vitals and their 'good' thresholds?
cards.answer: LCP (largest contentful paint) ≤ 2.5 s, INP (interaction to next paint) ≤ 200 ms, CLS (cumulative layout shift) ≤ 0.1.
cards.explanation: LCP is usually a slow hero image or a render-blocking resource; INP is long JavaScript tasks blocking the main thread; CLS is images and ads without reserved space. Fixes in order: set width/height on media, break up long tasks, preload the LCP resource.

cards.prompt: Server-side rendering vs client-side rendering
cards.answer: SSR sends HTML the browser can paint immediately; CSR sends a shell plus JavaScript that builds the page in the browser.

left.title: SSR / SSG
points: Fast first paint and reliable SEO
Hydration cost to make it interactive

right.title: CSR
points: Blank until JS parses and runs
Weaker on slow devices and networks

cards.explanation: Modern frameworks blend them: static generation for stable pages, streaming SSR for dynamic ones, client components only where interaction lives. The deciding question is whether the first paint must be meaningful without JavaScript.

modules.name: Storage, Origins & Security
modules.description: Cookies, storage APIs, same-origin policy, CORS and CSP.

cards.prompt: Cookies vs localStorage vs sessionStorage vs IndexedDB
cards.answer: Cookies are sent with every matching request; the storage APIs are client-only. localStorage persists, sessionStorage dies with the tab, IndexedDB stores large structured data asynchronously.

left.title: Cookies
points: The thing consent banners are about

right.title: Web storage / IndexedDB
points: Never sent to the server automatically
Readable by any script on the origin — not for secrets

cards.explanation: Session tokens belong in HttpOnly cookies so XSS cannot read them. Anything in localStorage is exposed to every script you load — which is also why a privacy notice should mention local storage, not only cookies.

cards.prompt: What is an origin, and what does the same-origin policy prevent?
cards.answer: An origin is the triple (scheme, host, port). The same-origin policy stops a document from reading data from another origin — its DOM, its responses, its storage — while still allowing embedding and navigation.
cards.explanation: It is the foundation of browser security: without it, any page could read your webmail in another tab. Note it blocks *reading*, not *sending* — which is exactly the gap CSRF exploits and SameSite cookies close.

cards.prompt: Your fetch fails with a CORS error. What is actually happening, and where do you fix it?
cards.answer: The browser made the request but refused to expose the response because the server did not send an appropriate `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`. The fix belongs on the server, never in the browser.
cards.explanation: A preflight `OPTIONS` is sent first for non-simple requests (custom headers, methods beyond GET/POST/HEAD, JSON content type). Credentialed requests require an explicit origin — not `*` — plus `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`. CORS relaxes the same-origin policy; it is not a security control on your data.

cards.prompt: What does a Content Security Policy do, and what makes one actually effective?
cards.answer: It tells the browser which sources may load and execute — scripts, styles, frames, connections. An effective policy is nonce- or hash-based with `strict-dynamic`, avoids `unsafe-inline` and `unsafe-eval`, and sets `object-src 'none'` and `base-uri 'self'`.
cards.explanation: CSP is defence in depth: it turns many XSS bugs into blocked script loads. Host allowlists are weak — a single CDN with an open JSONP endpoint defeats them — which is why Google's guidance moved to nonces. Roll out with `Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only` first.

cards.prompt: A session cookie should be `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=___` to block script access, plaintext transport and most cross-site sends.
cards.answer: Lax
cards.explanation: `SameSite=Lax` sends the cookie on top-level navigations but not on cross-site subrequests, which kills most CSRF — and it is what Chromium applies when a cookie omits the attribute. Set it explicitly rather than relying on browser defaults. Use `Strict` for high-value actions, and `None; Secure` only when a cookie genuinely must cross sites, as in embedded third-party contexts.

modules.name: HTTP in Practice
modules.description: Messages and headers, caching and validation, redirects, compression and real-time transports.

cards.prompt: What are the parts of an HTTP request and response?
cards.answer: Request: a method, a target path, the protocol version, headers (Host, Accept, Authorization, Cookie…) and an optional body. Response: a status code and reason, headers (Content-Type, Cache-Control, Set-Cookie…) and an optional body.
cards.explanation: HTTP is stateless — each request stands alone, and state rides along in cookies or tokens. Headers carry most of the protocol's power: content negotiation, caching, authentication, CORS and security policy. Browser DevTools' network panel shows every part of every exchange.

cards.prompt: How do `Cache-Control`, `ETag` and `If-None-Match` work together?
cards.answer: `Cache-Control` says whether and how long a response may be reused (`max-age=31536000, immutable`, `no-cache` = revalidate every time, `no-store` = never store, `private` = browser only). When stale, the browser revalidates with `If-None-Match: <etag>`; if unchanged the server answers `304 Not Modified` with no body.
cards.explanation: The standard strategy: content-hashed asset filenames (`app.3f9a1c.js`) cached for a year as immutable, and HTML served with `no-cache` so it always revalidates and points at the newest assets. `no-cache` does not mean "do not cache" — `no-store` does.

cards.answer: 301 and 308 are permanent — browsers and search engines cache them and transfer ranking. 302, 303 and 307 are temporary. 307 and 308 guarantee the method and body are preserved; 301 and 302 historically let clients change POST to GET, and 303 explicitly means "now GET this".

left.title: Permanent (301, 308)
points: Search engines move ranking to the new URL

cards.explanation: Use 308/301 for moved content and HTTP→HTTPS, 303 after a successful form POST (the Post/Redirect/Get pattern prevents duplicate submissions on refresh), and 307 for temporary moves of non-GET requests. Permanent redirects are cached hard, so test before shipping them.

cards.prompt: How is text content compressed over HTTP, and what should not be compressed?
cards.answer: The client advertises `Accept-Encoding: gzip, br, zstd`; the server compresses and labels it with `Content-Encoding`. Brotli typically beats gzip for text, especially when precompressed at build time at high levels.
cards.explanation: Compress HTML, CSS, JavaScript, JSON and SVG; skip already-compressed formats such as JPEG, PNG, WebP, video and zip. Compressing responses that mix secrets with attacker-controlled input can leak those secrets through response sizes (the BREACH attack).

cards.prompt: Polling vs Server-Sent Events vs WebSockets
cards.answer: Polling repeatedly asks for updates; SSE keeps one HTTP response open and streams server-to-client events; WebSockets upgrade to a full-duplex, message-based connection.

left.title: Polling / SSE
points: SSE: plain HTTP, auto-reconnect, event IDs

cards.explanation: Choose the simplest thing that fits: SSE for notifications, feeds and LLM token streaming (plain HTTP, automatic reconnect); WebSockets for chat, multiplayer and collaboration that need low-latency client messages too. Both need attention to proxies, timeouts and reconnection with backoff.

cards.prompt: Which HTTP security headers should most sites send?
cards.answer: `Strict-Transport-Security` (force HTTPS, with `includeSubDomains`), `Content-Security-Policy` (including `frame-ancestors` against clickjacking), `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin`, and `Permissions-Policy` to disable unused browser features.
cards.explanation: HSTS prevents SSL-stripping downgrades after the first visit (preloading covers the first). `frame-ancestors` supersedes `X-Frame-Options`. Check the result with a scanner such as Mozilla Observatory, and test CSP in report-only mode first.

modules.name: Building for the Browser
modules.description: Bundling and code splitting, images, workers and PWAs, the rendering frame, CDNs, SEO and progressive enhancement.

cards.prompt: What do bundlers do, and what are tree shaking and code splitting?
cards.answer: Bundlers (Vite, esbuild, webpack, Rollup) resolve imports, transpile, and emit optimised files. Tree shaking drops exports nothing imports, using ESM's static structure. Code splitting produces separate chunks loaded on demand with dynamic `import()`, so each page downloads only what it uses.
cards.explanation: Watch bundle size with an analyser: one careless import of a whole utility library or a date library's locales can double it. Side-effectful modules defeat tree shaking, which is what the `sideEffects` field in package.json declares.

resources.title: web.dev — Reduce JavaScript payloads with code splitting

cards.prompt: What are the essentials of shipping images on the web?
cards.answer: Modern formats (AVIF/WebP), correctly sized variants via `srcset` and `sizes`, explicit `width` and `height` to reserve space, `loading="lazy"` for below-the-fold images, and `fetchpriority="high"` (never lazy) for the LCP hero image.
cards.explanation: Images are usually the heaviest part of a page. Missing dimensions cause layout shift (CLS); lazy-loading the hero delays LCP. Every meaningful image needs `alt` text; decorative images get `alt=""` so screen readers skip them.

cards.prompt: Web Worker vs Service Worker
cards.answer: A Web Worker runs JavaScript on a background thread for CPU-heavy work, talking to the page via messages. A Service Worker is a proxy between the page and the network that intercepts requests, enabling offline support, caching strategies and push notifications — the heart of a PWA.

left.title: Web Worker
points: Created and owned by one page

right.title: Service Worker
points: Network proxy for the whole origin
HTTPS only; has its own update lifecycle

cards.explanation: Neither can touch the DOM. Service workers outlive pages and update on their own lifecycle, so a buggy one can pin users to stale assets — always version caches and plan an update and kill-switch path.

cards.prompt: What happens in one rendering frame, and what is `requestAnimationFrame` for?
cards.answer: Each frame (about 16.7 ms at 60 Hz): run tasks and microtasks, then `requestAnimationFrame` callbacks, then style, layout, paint and composite. rAF schedules visual updates to run just before the next paint, synchronised with the display.
cards.explanation: Animating with `setTimeout` drifts and can update twice or not at all in a frame; rAF also pauses in background tabs. Any task longer than ~50 ms blocks input and rendering — it shows up as poor INP — so split long work into chunks or move it to a worker.

cards.prompt: Users in Australia see slow loads from a server in Frankfurt. What helps most?
cards.answer: A CDN: edge servers near users cache static assets (and cacheable HTML/API responses), cutting round trips from ~300 ms to ~20 ms. TLS also terminates at the edge, so connection setup is local.
cards.explanation: Latency is bounded by the speed of light, so distance only shrinks by moving content closer. Cache keys and `Cache-Control` decide what the CDN may store; never cache personalised responses publicly. For dynamic, uncacheable data, regional replicas or edge compute are the next step.

cards.prompt: What technical basics matter most for search engines?
cards.answer: Crawlable, server-rendered HTML with a unique `<title>` and meta description per page, semantic headings, descriptive link text, a canonical URL for duplicate content, a sitemap and sensible `robots.txt`, fast Core Web Vitals, mobile-friendly layout, and structured data (JSON-LD) where relevant.
cards.explanation: Content that only appears after client-side JavaScript runs may be indexed late or not at all by some crawlers, which is a common reason to prefer SSR or static generation for public pages. Semantic, accessible HTML and good SEO largely overlap.

resources.title: Google Search Central — SEO starter guide

cards.prompt: Why should a checkout form still submit when the JavaScript bundle fails to load?
cards.answer: Progressive enhancement: build on a working HTML baseline (a real `<form>` with `action` and `method`), then layer JavaScript on top for a nicer experience. Scripts fail more than people think — flaky networks, blockers, CDN outages, old browsers — and core tasks should survive that.
cards.explanation: It also improves accessibility and resilience for free, and frameworks with server actions and form handling make it cheap. Decide per feature: rich editors can require JS; logging in, searching and paying generally should not.

cards.prompt: What does Subresource Integrity protect against?
cards.answer: A compromised CDN or third-party host serving modified JavaScript or CSS. `<script src="…" integrity="sha384-…" crossorigin="anonymous">` makes the browser refuse to run the file if its hash does not match the one you pinned.
cards.explanation: SRI only works for static files that never change at that URL, so it pairs with versioned library URLs. For first-party assets, content-hashed filenames on your own origin achieve the same thing. It is the browser-side counterpart of lockfile integrity hashes.
